basis.text: No writer of the time gives a clock reading for the charge. The reports of Rice, Chamberlain, Bane and Barnes (July and August 1863), read with Norton's computation (1913), bound it at about 17:30 at the earliest and before dusk; the only reading of an hour is the Maine commission's volume of 1898 (about 6:30 p.m., no source named). The two readings are an hour apart and nothing in the record separates them.

default.label: About 17:30 to 18:30: no report of 1863 gives a clock time; reasoned from the reports, with one later reading
default.basis_text: The early end (17:30) is reasoned from the reports of 1863: the Confederate attack on the brigade about 16:30 to 17:00 (Bane, Norton) and an hour of severe fighting before the bayonet order (Chamberlain; above half an hour in Rice). The late end (18:30) is the Maine commission's 'about 6:30 p. m.' (1898), whose basis is not named. Every reading is an 'about'; the window is wider than the 20 minutes by which the two armies' clocks reportedly differed, which is not applied.

animation.note: The picture draws the bayonet charge at 18:00, the midpoint of the window, because no source gives a point; it is not a documented time. The 17:30 of the plan and the first delegated window 16:00 to dusk stay selectable, and the window is shown with the animation.

default.note: A window, not a point: nothing in the record dates the charge to the minute. The plan's own timeline row for the charge names a range 17:30 to 18:15; the window here is half an hour longer at the late end, by the 1898 volume.

value.note: the early end of the window; no writer states it

inference.step: No writer of the time gives a clock reading for the charge. The reports start the fight at the brigade's order into position about 16:00 (Rice) and the Confederate attack on it about 16:30 to 17:00 (Bane, Norton), the first infantry attack coming as Chamberlain's line was formed, and give a length of 'above half an hour' to 'an hour' of severe fighting before the bayonet order (Rice, Chamberlain). 16:30 plus about an hour is 17:30: the earliest the charge can be placed by those reports, and the plan's value. Later fits within the same lengths run to about 18:00 or later.

weighing.summary: No writer of 1863 gives a clock time for the bayonet charge. Rice and Welch put the order into position about 4 p.m.; Bane and Norton put the Confederate attack on the brigade at 4:30 or between 4:30 and 5; Chamberlain has an hour of severe fighting after the flanking column came and then the order 'At that crisis, I ordered the bayonet', and Rice has above half an hour on the 20th Maine; both put the charge before dusk. Read together the reports give about 17:30 at the earliest. The only clock reading of the charge is later: a Maine volume of 1898 has about 6:30 p.m. and names no source. The reports and that volume are an hour apart and the record has nothing to choose between them, so the default is the window 17:30 to 18:30 (class irreducible, tier inferred), not a point.
weighing.who: Rice (44th New York, then the brigade), Chamberlain (20th Maine), Conner (44th New York), Welch (16th Michigan) and Woodward (83rd Pennsylvania) wrote as officers of Vincent's brigade on the hill; they are the best class of writing there is (reports within a month) and none gives a clock for the charge. Bane (4th Texas) wrote for the Confederates against the brigade's centre. Barnes, the division commander, does not say he was at the ledge and relays the brigade's reports. Norton was a private of the brigade, writing in 1913, and computes his 4:30 to 5 from the movements of the corps. Oates (15th Alabama) wrote in 1905. The Maine and Pennsylvania volumes are state commission books with no named writer for the passages.
weighing.when: The reports are of 6 July to 24 August 1863, 4 to 53 days after, the best class of writing the rubric knows, but they state lengths of time and the order into position, not an hour for the charge. Bane's report is of 9 July. Norton (1913), Oates (1905) and the state volumes (1898, 1914) are 35 to 51 years after. The one clock reading of the charge, in the Maine volume, is of the weakest class that gives one; it is not outweighed by a contrary report because the reports give none, and it is not a better one either because no basis is named. Woodward (6 July 1863) is the only writer of the time near an hour for the end of the fight and his other readings were disowned by him.
weighing.where: Chamberlain and Rice stood at the 20th Maine's position, Conner and Woodward at the 44th New York and the 83rd Pennsylvania next to it; Welch at the right end of the brigade. Bane's Texans attacked the brigade's centre and right, so his 4:30 dates the first attack, which came before the flanking column reached the 20th Maine (Chamberlain: the flanking column was seen after the assault on the centre was under way). The charge itself therefore came later than the first attack by the length of the fight at the 20th Maine's ledge. Barnes's 'nearly dark' and Chamberlain's 'At dusk' come after the charge.
weighing.how_knew: Chamberlain and Rice report their own commands and say what they saw; their lengths of time ('an hour', 'above half an hour') are estimates made with the action in mind and are not clock readings. Bane reports an order he received. Norton and the Maine volume do not say how they know: Norton computes, and the Maine volume names no source for 6:30. The monument inscription (about 5 p.m. for the brigade's arrival) names none either.
weighing.clock: The Union reports use the Union clock, Bane the Confederate, Norton and the state volumes no stated clock. The reported difference of about 20 minutes between the two armies' clocks is not applied; it is much smaller than the hour between the two ends of the window. Woodward's readings, taken on his own clock, are also disowned by him.
weighing.independence: The early end rests on four lines of knowledge that do not copy one another for the hours: Rice and Chamberlain (independent reports from the 44th New York and the 20th Maine), Bane (the Confederate side) and Norton (a computation from the corps's movements); but none of them states 17:30, which is a reasoned point, so the position is flagged weak. The late end rests on one line: the Maine volume (the same chapter dates the start about 4 p.m.; the monument inscription is a different volume and speaks to the arrival). Powell (1896) and Lossing (1868) follow the reports and do not give an hour; the Park Service texts give only 'twilight' for the later withdrawal and 'night fell' for the advance on Big Round Top; Gerrish (1882) has none.

source_panel_text: About 17:30 to 18:30 on Jul 2. No report of 1863 gives a clock time for the charge: Rice and Bane date the fight from about 4 to 4:30 p.m., and Chamberlain has an hour of hard fighting before his bayonet order. A Maine volume of 1898 says about 6:30 p.m., naming no source. The plan's 17:30 is the early end; 'no clock time' is also listed. Four other values are listed.

what_would_change_it: A report, letter or diary of 1863 to 1864 that gives a clock reading for the bayonet order or for the repulse in front of the 20th Maine (Spear, Morrill, Prince, Tozier or Melcher of the 20th Maine; the Oates or Law letters; the papers of the battlefield commission or the Bachelder papers) would replace the window. So would the Maine commission's source for 'about 6:30 p. m.', or the key (SS2) the plan prints for 17:30. Two independent writers of the time for one hour would make the conflict weighted.
owner_note: The first delegated default (about 17:30, window 16:00 to dusk) is replaced by a narrower window, 17:30 to 18:30, drawn at 18:00; nothing is deleted. If the owner wants a point instead of a window, the candidates are 17:30 (the plan's value, an inference) and 18:30 (the Maine volume): no source of the time supports either as a point. The charge is not an arrival and is not read by the arrival gate.
